mainTopic: Who gets the שבח (improvement) when land or a stolen item is improved, and which changes (שינוי) let a thief acquire what he stole.
overview: The amud opens by finishing an answer to two rulings of שמואל that seem to contradict each other: does a בעל חוב collect the שבח a buyer added to the land? The גמרא says it depends on how much he is owed. רבינא challenges this, and רב אשי defends it by explaining that the field was an אפותיקי. רבא then rules that a גזלן who improves a stolen item and sells it or leaves it to heirs passes the improvement along. A buyer who improves it himself also keeps the improvement, because a seller hands over all his rights. רבא also asks about a גוי who improved the item, and the question ends in תיקו. Next, רב פפא and רבא teach when changing a stolen palm tree or palm frond counts as a real שינוי that lets the thief acquire it. The test is whether it gets a new name, and a change that can be undone does not count. Finally, רב פפא asks about a לולב whose תיומת split, and the גמרא begins bringing a proof that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: It depends on how much the creditor is owed
steps.stepSummary: The two rulings of שמואל do not contradict each other. If the debt covers the land plus the improvement, the creditor takes both. If the debt covers only the land, he does not take the improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ruling is where the creditor is owed enough to cover the land and the improvement. That ruling is where he is owed only enough to cover the land.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its answer to a contradiction between two rulings of שמואל about whether a בעל חוב collects the שבח (improvement) that a buyer added to the land.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer divides the cases by the size of the debt. If the debt equals the land plus the שבח, the creditor collects everything. If the debt equals only the original land, he collects just that, and the improvement stays with the buyer. So both rulings of שמואל are correct, each in its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: He is owed by him (the creditor is owed money by the debtor)
Amount or measure
Land
Improvement, the added value

phrases.english: This is where he is owed by him
phrases.notes: "He" is the creditor, and "him" is the debtor who sold the land.

phrases.english: the amount of the land and the improvement;
that is where he is not owed by him
except the amount of the land.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא דְּמַסֵּיק בֵּיהּ כְּשִׁיעוּר אַרְעָא וּשְׁבָחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues an answer that began before this section, resolving a contradiction between two rulings of שמואל.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא based on the size of the debt)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: שמואל seemed to contradict himself about whether a creditor collects the שבח.
steps.terutzMaskana: The creditor collects the שבח only when his debt is large enough to cover it.

steps.title: The buyer should be able to keep land worth his improvement
steps.stepSummary: רבינא argues that this answer only works for one opinion. According to the view that a buyer may pay off the creditor with money, the buyer could say: give me a piece of land worth my improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to him: This works for the one who says that a buyer who has money still cannot pay off the creditor. But for the one who says a buyer with money can pay off the creditor, let the buyer say: 'If I had money, I would pay you off for the whole field. Now, at least give me a piece of land equal to my improvement!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא challenges the answer from step 1. He argues that, according to one opinion, even when the debt is large the creditor should not get the improvement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a מחלוקת about whether a לוקח can pay the creditor cash instead of giving up the land. If he can, his right to the land is strong. So he should at least be able to keep a piece of land matching his שבח instead of losing it to the creditor. That would undo the first half of step 1's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: This works well for the one who says (it fits one opinion, but not the other)
Buyer
Creditor
He is able to remove (pay off) him
Money (literally, coins)
A measure of land, about a סאה's worth of field

phrases.english: He said to him: This works well according to the one who says:
if the buyer has money,

phrases.aramaic: לָא מָצֵי מְסַלֵּק לֵיהּ לְבַעַל חוֹב, שַׁפִּיר.
phrases.english: he cannot remove the creditor; then it is fine.
But according to the one who says:
if the buyer has money,
he can remove the creditor,
let him say to him:
If I had money,
I would remove you from the whole land;
now, give me a griva of land,
the amount of my improvement!
phrases.notes: He means: I can't pay for the whole field, so let me keep a piece of it equal to what I added.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the first half of the answer in step 1, where the creditor takes the land and the improvement.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a creditor owed enough collects the שבח too.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a buyer may pay the creditor cash instead of giving up the land, he should also be able to keep a part of the land equal to his improvement.

steps.title: The field was set aside as the only source of payment
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי answers that the case is an אפותיקי. The debtor told the creditor he could collect only from this field, so the buyer cannot pay him off with anything else.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said to him: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the debtor made this field an אפותיקי for him, telling him: 'You will be paid only from this field.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי defends the earlier answer by narrowing the case to a field that was specially set aside to pay this debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With an אפותיקי, the creditor's claim is attached to this exact field and nothing else. So even under the opinion that a buyer may usually pay cash, here he cannot push the creditor off the field or keep part of it. The creditor takes the whole field, improvement included, when his debt covers it.

keyTerms.meaning: With what case are we dealing here? (used to narrow a ruling to a specific case)
A field set aside as the only source for paying a debt
Repayment

steps.whatToRemember: The rule that a creditor collects the שבח when owed enough applies to an אפותיקי, where the debt is attached only to that field.

phrases.english: He said to him: With what are we dealing here?
Such as where he made it an apotiki for him,
phrases.notes: The debtor set this one field aside to pay this debt.

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲמַר לֵיהּ: לֹא יְהֵא לְךָ פֵּרָעוֹן
phrases.english: that he said to him: You shall not have repayment
except from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבינא's challenge from step 2 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: אוקימתא (narrowing the case to an אפותיקי)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The buyer could keep land worth his improvement, since he may pay the creditor off.
steps.terutzMaskana: In an אפותיקי the creditor's claim is attached only to this field, so the buyer cannot pay him off in any other way.

steps.title: A robber who improves an item passes the improvement to a buyer or heir
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that when a גזלן improves a stolen item and then sells it or leaves it to heirs, the improvement goes along with it to the buyer or heir.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If someone robbed, improved the item, and sold it, or robbed, improved it, and left it to his heirs, then he sold what he improved, and he left to his heirs what he improved.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new statement of רבא about a stolen item that was improved and then sold or passed on to heirs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The improvement a גזלן adds belongs to him, and when he sells or bequeaths the item, that right passes to the לוקח or the יורש. So if the owner wants his item back, he must pay the buyer or heir for the improvement. This connects to the earlier topic of who owns the שבח.

keyTerms.meaning: He robbed
He improved (added value)
He left it as an inheritance

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying the buyer or heir keeps the stolen item itself. He is saying they get the value of the improvement.

phrases.english: Rava said:
If he robbed, improved it, and sold it,
or robbed, improved it, and bequeathed it,
what he improved, he sold;
what he improved, he bequeathed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new statement about a stolen item that was improved, moving on from the creditor discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A גזלן's right to the improvement passes to whoever buys the item from him or inherits it.

steps.title: What if the buyer improved the stolen item?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks what the law is when a buyer of a stolen item improves it himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: If the buyer improved the stolen item, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises a new question. He already ruled that a thief's improvement passes to his buyer, and now he asks about an improvement the buyer made himself. The גמרא is setting up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 4 the thief made the improvement and then sold the item. Here the thief sells an item that has not been improved, and the buyer does the improving. The question is whether the buyer gets the same right the thief would have had.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked; he raised a question he was unsure about
He improved it; he raised its value
Buyer

phrases.english: Rava asked:
If the buyer improved it, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes רבא's ruling about a thief's improvement and asks about a new case, where the buyer is the one who improved the item.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a buyer who improved a stolen item get to keep the value of his improvement, as the thief himself would?

steps.title: רבא answers: the seller passes on all his rights
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers his own question: a seller transfers every right he has, so the buyer gets the thief's right to the improvement.
steps.simpleTranslation: After he asked it, he answered it: What does the first person sell to the second? Every right that will come into his hands.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers his own question. The buyer keeps the improvement he made.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whenever someone sells, he hands over all of his rights to the buyer. The thief would have kept the value of any improvement he made, so the buyer has that same right. Because the buyer stands in the thief's place, his own improvement is his.

keyTerms.meaning: He resolved it; he answered the question
A right or legal claim

steps.whatToRemember: A buyer stands in the seller's place: whatever rights the seller had, the buyer now has.

phrases.english: After he asked it, he went back and answered it:
What does the first sell to the second?
phrases.notes: The 'first' is the seller (here, the thief), and the 'second' is the buyer.

phrases.english: Every right that will come into his hands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question raised in Step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The buyer keeps his improvement, because a seller passes on every right he has, including the thief's right to improvements.

steps.title: What if a גוי improved the stolen item?
steps.stepSummary: רבא asks what the law is when a גוי is the one who improved a stolen item.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא asked: If a גוי improved it, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא raises another question, this time about a גוי who improved stolen property. The next steps will challenge the question itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule that lets a thief keep his improvement is a rabbinic enactment. רבא wants to know whether that enactment also applies when a גוי made the improvement.

keyTerms.meaning: A non-Jew

phrases.english: Rava asked:
If a gentile improved it, what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new question about improvements, now involving a גוי.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the rabbinic rule that lets the improver keep the improvement apply when a גוי did the improving?

steps.title: Would the חכמים make an enactment to benefit a גוי?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא מדפתי challenges the question: the חכמים would never set up a special enactment for a גוי's benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא מדפתי said to רבינא: Should we get up and make an enactment for a גוי?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אחא מדפתי attacks רבא's question. To him, the answer is obvious.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Letting a thief keep his improvement is a special rabbinic enactment. The חכמים made it for Jews, so it makes no sense to ask whether it helps a גוי. The question seems to have nothing to ask about.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic enactment; a special rule the חכמים set up
Shall we get up and do

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא מִדִּפְתִּי לְרָבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rav Acha of Difti said to Ravina:
Shall we get up and make an enactment for a gentile?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the question asked in Step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's question about a גוי who improved stolen property
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The improvement rule is a rabbinic enactment, and the חכמים do not make enactments for the benefit of a גוי. So the question has an obvious answer.

steps.title: The case is where the גוי sold it to a Jew
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that the question is about a גוי who sold the improved item to a Jew.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: The question is only needed where the גוי sold it to a Jew.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא defends the question by changing the case. Now a Jew is involved, as the buyer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Nobody is asking about helping the גוי himself. The question is whether the Jewish buyer, who bought from the גוי, gets to keep the improvement.

keyTerms.meaning: It is only needed for; the question only applies to the following case
He sold it

phrases.english: He said to him: It is only needed
for a case where he sold it to a Jew.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 8 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was about helping a גוי, which makes no sense.
steps.terutzMaskana: The question is about a Jewish buyer who bought the item from the גוי who improved it.

steps.title: Someone who buys from a גוי is like the גוי
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back: a buyer only has the rights of his seller, so someone who buys from a גוי is treated like the גוי.
steps.simpleTranslation: In the end, one who comes through a גוי is just like the גוי!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבינא's answer. The new case still does not seem to raise a real question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: From Step 6 we know that a buyer only gets the rights his seller had. The גוי had no right to the improvement, since the enactment was not made for him, so he had nothing to pass on to the Jewish buyer. Once again, the answer looks obvious.

keyTerms.meaning: In the end; after all
One who comes through; one who gets his rights from

phrases.english: In the end, one who comes through a gentile
is just like the gentile!

steps.triggerLanguage: סוֹף סוֹף, הַבָּא מֵחֲמַת גּוֹי הֲרֵי הוּא כְּגוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the case offered in Step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבינא's case of a גוי who sold the item to a Jew
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A buyer has only the rights of his seller. The גוי had no rights under the enactment, so the Jew who bought from him has none either.

steps.title: Jew, then גוי, then Jew: does the enactment apply?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא narrows the case again: a Jew stole the item and sold it to a גוי, the גוי improved it, and then sold it to another Jew. Does the enactment apply because Jews are at both ends, or not, because a גוי was in the middle?
steps.simpleTranslation: It is only needed where a Jew stole it and sold it to a גוי, the גוי improved it, and then the גוי sold it to a Jew. What is the law? Do we say that since there was a Jew at the start and a Jew at the end, the חכמים made their enactment? Or perhaps, since there is a גוי in the middle, the חכמים did not make an enactment for him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא saves רבא's question by finding a case where the doubt is real. It then lays out both sides of the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the chain starts with a Jewish thief and ends with a Jewish buyer, so you might think the enactment should apply. On the other hand, the improvement itself was made while the גוי owned the item, and the enactment was never made for a גוי. Each side has a good argument.

keyTerms.meaning: He stole it
At the start; originally
In the middle
Or perhaps

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix this up with Step 9. There the item came straight from a גוי. Here a Jew stole it first, a גוי improved it, and a Jew bought it at the end. Only this three-person chain leaves a real doubt.

phrases.english: It is only needed where a Jew stole it
phrases.notes: The letter in square brackets is part of the corrected wording, which reads 'stole it'.

phrases.english: and sold it to him,
and the gentile improved it,
and then the gentile sold it to a Jew.
What is the law?
Do we say: since at the start it was a Jew
and at the end it is a Jew,
the Sages made the enactment;

phrases.aramaic: אוֹ דִלְמָא כֵּיוָן דְּאִיכָּא גּוֹי בָּאֶמְצַע –
phrases.english: or perhaps, since there is a gentile in the middle,
the Sages did not make an enactment for him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 10 by finding a narrower case, then states the doubt in that case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (אוקימתא) to one where the doubt is real
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any case involving a גוי has an obvious answer.
steps.terutzMaskana: When a Jew is at both ends of the chain and a גוי is in the middle, it is a real question whether the enactment applies.

steps.title: The question stays unresolved
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves רבא's question unanswered: תיקו.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא ends this discussion without an answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Neither side of the doubt in Step 11 is proven. The question of a Jew, then a גוי, then a Jew is left as an open question.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stand; the question is left unresolved

steps.whatToRemember: The improvement rule is a rabbinic enactment for Jews. Whether it applies when a גוי improved the item in the middle of a Jewish chain stays an open question (תיקו).

phrases.english: Let it stand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the doubt raised in Step 11 without deciding it.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: There is no ruling on whether the enactment applies when a גוי improved the item between a Jewish thief and a Jewish buyer.

steps.title: A cut-down palm tree is still a palm tree
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that a thief who cuts down a stolen palm tree does not acquire it, even if he moves it onto his own land, because it is still called a 'palm tree'.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: Someone who steals a palm tree from his friend and cuts it down does not acquire it, even if he throws it from that land onto his own land. Why? At first it was called a 'palm tree', and now it is also called a 'palm tree'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic: what counts as a big enough change (שינוי) for a thief to own what he stole. רב פפא gives a first example.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A thief only acquires a stolen item through a real change, and here the test is whether the item now has a new name. A cut-down palm tree keeps the name 'palm tree', so nothing has really changed. Moving it onto his own land does not help him either.

keyTerms.meaning: Palm tree
He cut it down
He acquires; he becomes the owner
It is called

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a clear test for שינוי: if the item still has the same name, the thief has not acquired it and must return the item itself.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מַאן דִּגְזַל דִּיקְלָא מֵחַבְרֵיהּ וְקַטְלֵיהּ,
phrases.english: This one who stole a palm tree from his friend and cut it down,
even though he threw it from the land
onto his own land,
does not acquire it.
What is the reason?
At first it was called a 'palm tree',
and now it is also called a 'palm tree'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic: what counts as a change that lets a thief acquire the stolen item.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cutting down a stolen palm tree is not a real change, because it keeps the name 'palm tree'. The thief does not acquire it, even if he moves it onto his own land.

steps.title: Palm tree logs are still 'palm tree logs'
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא adds that even cutting the stolen palm tree into logs is not a real change, because they are called 'palm tree logs'.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he made the palm tree into logs, he does not acquire it, because now they are still called 'palm tree logs'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא continues his ruling with a bigger change: cutting the tree into logs. Even this is not enough.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think that logs are a new kind of object. But the name still points back to the original palm tree, so this does not count as a real change of name, and the thief still does not acquire it.

keyTerms.meaning: Logs; sections of a tree trunk
In any case; at least

steps.whatToRemember: A change only lets a thief acquire the item if it gets a new name. 'Palm tree' and 'palm tree logs' both still carry the original name.

phrases.english: A palm tree that he made into logs,
phrases.notes: Some versions say the word in round brackets; the corrected wording uses the word in square brackets. Both mean 'he made it'.

phrases.english: he does not acquire it.
Now, in any case, they are called 'palm tree logs'.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends רב פפא's ruling to a bigger change: cutting the tree into logs.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Cutting a stolen palm tree into logs is still not a real change, because they are called 'palm tree logs'. The thief does not acquire it.

steps.title: Logs to beams, big beams to small beams, beams to boards
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא continues: logs made into beams are acquired. Big beams cut into small beams are not acquired. Beams cut into boards are acquired.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he stole logs and made them into beams, he acquires them. If he stole big beams and made them into small beams, he does not acquire them. If he made them into boards, he acquires them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא continues רב פפא's list of rules about stolen wood. It shows which kinds of cutting count as a real change and which do not.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test is the same as with the palm tree: does the object get a new name? Logs that become beams have a new name, so the thief acquires them. Big beams that become small beams are still called 'beams', so he does not. Boards have a new name, so cutting beams into boards counts as a change.

keyTerms.meaning: Logs, rough cut pieces of a tree trunk
Beams
Boards, thin cut planks
He acquires it (the thief now owns it and pays money instead)

steps.confusionAlert: Cutting something smaller is not always a change. Big beams into small beams does not count, because the name stays 'beams'. What matters is the name, not the amount of work.

phrases.english: Logs that he made into beams: he acquires them.
Large beams that he made
into small beams: he does not acquire them.
If he made them into boards: he acquires them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב פפא's rules from Steps 13-14, moving from palm tree logs to beams and boards.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Logs to beams: acquired. Big beams to small beams: not acquired. Beams to boards: acquired.

steps.title: Palm frond to leaves, leaves to broom, broom to rope
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that a palm frond stripped into leaves is acquired, and leaves made into a broom are acquired. A broom twisted into a rope is not acquired, because the rope can be undone back into a broom.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: If someone stole a palm frond and made it into leaves, he acquires it. At first it was called a 'palm frond' and now it is called 'leaves'. If he made leaves into a broom, he acquires them. At first they were 'leaves' and now they are a 'broom'. If he made a broom into a rope, he does not acquire it. Why? Because he can untwist it, and it will be a broom again.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new chain of three rules about a stolen palm frond. Each step turns it into something with a new name.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first two changes count because the object gets a new name: frond to 'leaves', and leaves to 'broom'. The third change has a new name too ('rope'), but it still does not count. The rope can be untwisted back into a broom, and a change that can go back is not a real change.

keyTerms.meaning: A palm frond (a לולב), still whole
Palm leaves stripped off the frond
A broom made of palm leaves
A rope or chain twisted from the leaves
To take apart or undo

steps.whatToRemember: Two tests together: (1) does the object now have a new name? (2) can the change be undone? A new name that can easily go back to the old form (broom to rope) is not a real change.
steps.whyThisMatters: This adds a second rule next to the 'new name' test. A change that can go back to the earlier form (שינוי החוזר) does not let the thief acquire.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דִּגְזַל לוּלִיבָּא
phrases.english: רבא said: one who stole a palm frond
and made it into leaves: he acquires it.
phrases.notes: He stripped the leaves off the spine of the frond.

phrases.english: For at first it was called a 'palm frond',
and now it is called 'leaves'.
Leaves that he made into a broom: he acquires them.
At first they were 'leaves', and now they are a 'broom'.
A broom that he made into a rope: he does not acquire it.
What is the reason?
Because he can go back and undo it, and it becomes a broom again.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דִּגְזַל לוּלִיבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same 'new name' test as רב פפא, but with a palm frond. It also adds a new limit: a change that can be undone does not count.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Frond to leaves and leaves to broom: acquired. Broom to rope: not acquired, because the rope can be undone back into a broom.

steps.title: What if the twin center leaf of a לולב split?
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא asks what the law is if the תיומת (the twin center leaf of a לולב) became split.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא asked: If the twin center leaf split, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: Still talking about palm fronds, רב פפא asks a new question. What happens if the twin leaf at the top of the לולב splits? This opens a new question that the גמרא will now try to answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תיומת is the center leaf at the top of the לולב, made of two halves joined together. רב פפא wants to know whether a split there counts as a real change. The open point is whether splitting it is treated like removing it, or is too small to matter.

keyTerms.meaning: He asks a question he does not know the answer to
The twin center leaf at the top of a לולב, made of two joined halves
It became split or divided
What is the law?

phrases.english: רב פפא asked:
If the twin leaf split, what is the law?
phrases.notes: The two halves of the center leaf came apart, but the leaf was not taken off.

steps.triggerLanguage: בָּעֵי רַב פָּפָּא: נֶחְלְקָה הַתְּיוֹמֶת, מַהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבא just discussed palm fronds. רב פפא now asks about a smaller change to a לולב: a split center leaf.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does splitting the תיומת count as a real change, the same as if it were removed?

steps.title: A teaching about a removed twin leaf
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a teaching from רבי מתון in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי: if the תיומת was removed, the לולב is פסול.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי מתון said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי: If the twin leaf was removed, the לולב is not kosher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to answer רב פפא's question with a known teaching. It is setting up a comparison between a removed twin leaf and a split one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The teaching only says that a removed תיומת makes the לולב פסול. It does not speak about a split one. The גמרא will next have to decide whether a split counts the same as a removal.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear, used to bring a source that may answer the question
It was removed or taken off
Not kosher for use (here, for the מצוה of לולב)

steps.confusionAlert: This teaching is about a removed leaf, not a split one. The proof is not finished yet. The גמרא still has to show that split is treated like removed.

phrases.english: Come and hear, for רבי מתון said
in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי:
If the twin leaf was removed, it is unfit.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע, דְּאָמַר רַבִּי מָתוּן אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tries to answer רב פפא's question from Step 17 with a related teaching about a removed תיומת.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a split תיומת is treated as a real change
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי מתון in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי: a removed תיומת makes the לולב פסול
